The sum of the resistance and reactance components exhibited by these elements is called impedance, which is expressed in complex form (Z = Z′ + jZ′′). Here, the real part (Z′) represents the resistance component related to energy dissipation, while the imaginary part (Z′′) signifies the reactance component associated with energy storage and release [4]. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) enables the determination of impedance values at each fre­ quency by applying AC voltage over a wide frequency range and measuring the resulting current response [5]. Through this approach, R, C, L values constituting the equivalent circuit can be quantitatively separated, allowing systematic analysis of key electrochemical parameters such as ohmic losses, charge transfer rates, and interfacial capacitance of the system [6].

## Introduction

Most electrochemical systems can be represented by an equivalent circuit consisting of a combination of resistors (R), capacitors (C), and inductors (L). These three basic elements all serve to impede current flow within the sys­ tem, each reflecting distinct physicochemical mechanisms [1]. Resistance represents the ohmic resistance (RΩ) associ­ ated with ionic conduction in the electrolyte and the charge transfer resistance (Rct) at the electrode surface, maintain­ ing constant values regardless of frequency [2]. Capacitors reflect the charge storage capability of the electric double layer (EDL) formed at the electrode–electrolyte interface, impeding current flow particularly in the high-frequency

Abstract Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is a powerful non-destructive analytical technique that enables quantitative analysis of complex electrochemical processes occurring at electrode–electrolyte interfaces in electrochemical systems. This review introduces the fundamental principles of EIS analysis and equivalent circuit modeling, and systematically presents methodologies for their application to next-generation solar cells and photoelectrochemical (PEC) hydrogen pro­ duction systems. In electrochemistry-based solar cells such as dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs) and quantum dot-sensi­ tized solar cells (QDSCs), EIS enables the separate analysis of electron transport characteristics within photoelectrodes, charge recombination at interfaces, and counter electrode catalyst activity, providing key design parameters for improv­ ing photoconversion efficiency. Furthermore, in PEC cell-based hydrogen production systems, quantitative evaluation of charge transfer resistance, charge recombination characteristics, and mass transfer rates at semiconductor photoelectrodes allows for the derivation of performance optimization strategies for photoanodes and photocathodes. Through various research cases, this review demonstrates that EIS analysis is a valuable tool for simultaneously characterizing both ther­ modynamic and kinetic aspects of electrochemical solar cells and PEC hydrogen production devices, thereby providing practical directions for performance enhancement and commercialization of PEC energy conversion technologies.

Among these technologies, photoelectrochemi­ cal (PEC) energy devices such as PEC solar cells and PEC hydrogen production have been regarded as promis­ ing approaches because of their low-cost and relatively high efficiencies [8–14]. As a green hydrogen production method, PEC hydrogen production cells utilize electron– hole pairs generated by light absorption at semiconductor photoelectrodes directly for water splitting reactions, and are evaluated as efficient systems due to the integration of light absorption and electrochemical reactions within a single device [15]. In PEC systems, the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) or hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) pro­ ceeds at the photoanode or photocathode, respectively, and this technology is regarded as essential for achieving car­ bon neutrality as it enables hydrogen production using only solar energy without fossil fuels [16].

Moreover, recently, PEC solar cells that can be fabricated with low-cost materials have attracted attention as alterna­ tives to expensive crystalline silicon solar cells [17, 18]. Representative examples of PEC solar cells, such as dyesensitized solar cells (DSSCs) and quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSCs), are based on typical electrochemical systems, consisting of working electrodes, counter elec­ trodes, and electrolytes [19].

These PEC energy devices can be represented by equiv­ alent circuits for each electrode and interface, and EIS enables quantitative determination of each electrochemical parameter value. Through this approach, the PEC proper­ ties and photovoltaic properties of solar cells can be sys­ tematically characterized. Impedance analysis is a highly useful analytical technique as it can simultaneously analyze both thermodynamic aspects, such as energy level changes of photoelectrodes in contact with electrolytes, and kinetic aspects, including electron transport characteristics within photoelectrodes, charge recombination at interfaces, and counter electrode catalyst activity [20–23]. Meanwhile, PEC hydrogen production cells are also systems where complex PEC reactions occur at the photoelectrode-elec­ trolyte interface, and impedance analysis enables quantita­ tive evaluation of Rct, charge recombination characteristics, mass transfer properties, and catalytic activity for the OER at photoanodes or the HER at photocathodes [24].

This mini review presents methodologies for analyz­ ing the photovoltaic and electrochemical characteristics of electrochemical solar cells and PEC hydrogen produc­ tion systems using impedance analysis, and examines their application potential through actual research cases.

## Fundamental principles of EIS analysis for PEC energy devices

Impedance spectra of PEC solar cells

*Figure  1a illustrates the schematic structure of a DSSC. The DSSC utilizes a photoanode where dye molecules are adsorbed as a single atomic layer onto a nanostructured, porous TiO2 film. The counter electrode is typically fabri­ cated by coating platinum (Pt) onto a transparent conduct­ ing oxide (TCO) glass substrate, such as fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO). Furthermore, the device is constructed by injecting a liquid electrolyte containing the iodide/triiodide (I−/I3*

−) redox couple. As shown in Fig.  1b, the structure of the QDSC is highly similar. Instead of dye molecules, nanosized semiconductor particles, known as quantum dots (QDs), are adsorbed and used as the photosensitizer. Generally, copper sulfide (Cu2S) is employed as the coun­ ter electrode catalyst instead of Pt, and the device is driven by the movement of a polysulfide redox couple within the electrolyte.

The typical impedance spectrum (Nyquist plot) of these electrochemical solar cells is presented in Fig. 1c. It gener­ ally consists of three semicircles, each corresponding to a distinct interface or mass transport phenomenon. The first semicircle, Z1, appears at the highest AC frequencies and originates from the impedance at the counter electrode/ electrolyte interface. The second semicircle, Z2, is observed in the intermediate frequency range, corresponding to the impedance at the working electrode/electrolyte interface. Finally, the feature observed in the lowest frequency range, Z3, represents the impedance associated with the diffusion of the redox couple within the electrolyte.

The equivalent circuit used to interpret this impedance spectrum in solar cells is shown in Fig.  1d. This model includes several key elements. Firstly, the series resistance (Rs) represents the overall DC resistance within the device (e.g., sheet resistance of FTO, contact resistance), and its value is derived from the intercept point of the high-fre­ quency semicircle on the Z′ axis of the impedance spectrum. Secondly, the counter electrode impedance (RPt) is typically modeled by a parallel combination of Rct,CE and a constant phase element (CPE1). The term CPE is the abbreviation for "constant phase element," and it is utilized instead of a pure C component when dealing with electrodes having high sur­ face roughness, such as porous films, to account for the nonideal capacitive behavior caused by surface heterogeneity. The working electrode impedance is similarly modeled by another parallel combination of Rct,WE and CPE2 (or a simi­ lar structure, depending on the phenomenon being isolated). Lastly, the circuit includes the Warburg impedance (W) to account for the diffusion of the redox species within the

By utilizing this equivalent circuit, the impedance spectrum is fitted, and the resulting values for each elec­ trochemical parameter are obtained. This process allows for the systematic characterization of the cell’s PEC and photovoltaic properties, which are directly related to these parameters. Impedance spectra of PEC hydrogen production cells

The Nyquist plot of PEC hydrogen production cells, shown in Fig. 2a, can exhibit various forms depending on the photoelectrode structure and measurement conditions, but fundamentally consists of multiple semicircles. In the

high-frequency region, a real-axis intercept associated with Rs appears, reflecting the resistance of the electrode, elec­ trolyte, and external connections. In the mid-frequency region, a semicircle arising from Rct and Cdl at the photo­ electrode/electrolyte interface is observed. In the low-fre­ quency region, W related to ion diffusion and mass transfer processes in the electrolyte may appear, which is particu­ larly pronounced in dark conditions or diffusion-dominated systems [27–30]. Conversely, under illumination condi­ tions, the charge transfer process becomes dominant due to photogenerated charges, and the diffusion component may become relatively less significant.

The equivalent circuit for interpreting the impedance spectrum of PEC cells is fundamentally modeled, as can be observed in Fig. 2b. Here, Rs represents the series resistance within the device and is expressed as the value at the point where the semicircle begins on the Z' axis in the impedance spectrum. Rct signifies the charge transfer resistance at the photoelectrode/electrolyte interface, reflecting the kinetic characteristics of water splitting reactions OER or HER. ## Case studies of EIS analysis for PEC energy devices

EIS analysis of PEC solar cells

In DSSCs, the operating characteristics of the photo- and counter electrodes can significantly change depending on the composition and chemical properties of the injected electrolyte. While the photoelectrode is typically based on a porous TiO2 film, various metal oxides such as ZnO, SnO2, and Nb2O5 have also been actively investigated for DSSCs due to their faster electron transport characteristics com­ pared to TiO2.

*Table 1 demonstrates how the photovoltaic perfor­ mance of SnO2-based DSSCs varies with the concentra­ tion of 4-tert-butyl pyridine (TBP) in the electrolyte. TBP molecules adsorb onto the surface of the photoelectrode’s metal oxide, impeding the access of positive charges from the electrolyte. Consequently, this mitigates electron recom­ bination between the photoelectrode and the redox couple, leading to an increase in the cell’s open-circuit voltage VOC. The role of TBP is particularly critical for SnO2 electrodes, which typically exhibit much faster electron recombina­ tion with the electrolyte than conventional TiO2 electrodes. When diffusion processes are dominant in the low-frequency region, particularly under dark conditions or low-light envi­ ronments, W can be added to the equivalent circuit, such as the structure shown in Fig. 2c, to quantify ion mass transfer characteristics [31, 32].

When the structure of PEC cells becomes complex, for example, when protective layers are introduced or multi­ layer structures are present, simple single RC parallel cir­ cuits may be insufficient for adequate description. In such cases, complex equivalent circuit such as Maxwell, Voigt, or Nested circuits are employed, and Maxwell circuits in particular have been reported to best describe the electro­ chemical behavior of actual PEC cells under hydrogen evo­ lution conditions [29]. These circuits combine multiple RC elements in series or parallel to enable independent analysis of electrochemical processes at different interfaces (e.g., photoelectrode/protective layer interface, protective layer/ electrolyte interface).

By fitting impedance spectra using these equivalent cir­ cuits, the values of each electrochemical parameter can be quantitatively obtained. The Rct value directly reflects the catalytic activity of the photoelectrode, with smaller Rct values indicating faster charge transfer and higher catalytic activity. CPE values are related to the effective surface area of the photoelectrode and the charge storage capability of the interface, while the Warburg coefficient represents the ion diffusion rate in the electrolyte. ## Conclusion

EIS is a crucial and versatile tool for analyzing and opti­ mizing next-generation PEC devices, including DSSCs, QDSCs, and PEC hydrogen production cells. EIS effec­ tively separates kinetic, thermodynamic, and mass transport phenomena, providing key mechanistic insights beyond standard J-V analysis. In summary, EIS is an essential diag­ nostic tool that enables researchers to quantify fundamen­ tal electrochemical parameters (Rct, Cμ, Rs) and correlate them directly with material and interface properties. This mechanistic understanding is vital for the rational design and development of highly efficient, next-generation PEC energy conversion devices.

To elucidate the effect of defect density in CISe QDs on PEC hydrogen production performance, EIS analysis was conducted on CISe QD/TiO2 photoanodes synthesized by controlling the In/Cu ratio. Figure 8a presents the Nyquist plot of the CISe QDs/TiO2 photoanodes with different In/ Cu ratios. The equivalent circuit consists of a Rs and an RC circuit representing the charge transfer characteristics at the photoanode/electrolyte interface. Specifically, the interfa­ cial Rct is directly related to the rate of charge transfer at the interface. The Rct values obtained through fitting decreased in the order of CISe 5 > 1 > 2 > 4 > 3 (Table 2), and this trend was consistent under both light and dark conditions.

These results are consistent with the time-resolved pho­ toluminescence (TRPL) analysis, demonstrating that lower Cμ vacancy density leads to longer charge carrier lifetime and higher charge carrier mobility, resulting in more effi­ cient charge separation and hole transfer at the interface.
